function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that you can drop into the **`nodejs-welcome`** repository.  
After adding them, just commit and push – the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build the image whenever you push to `main`.

---

## 1. Dockerfile (Node.js)

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the dependency files first – this allows Docker cache to be reused
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and contains the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * Installing dependencies before copying the rest of the code lets Docker cache the `npm ci` step.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML

We’ll use the helper function `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` to generate a minimal deployment + service.  
(If you prefer to write it by hand, the output below is what the function would produce.)

```yaml
# kubernetes.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: node:18-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app on port 3000 inside the cluster.  
> * Uses a `ClusterIP` service – change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI – Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑platform builder)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or GitHub Container Registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image and push it to Docker Hub
      - name: Build & Push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: yourdockerhubusername/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

### Secrets you’ll need

| Secret | What to put |
|--------|-------------|
| `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` | Your Docker Hub username |
| `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | A Docker Hub access token (or password) |

> **Tip** – If you prefer GitHub Container Registry, replace the login step with `docker/login-action@v2` using `registry: ghcr.io` and adjust the `tags` accordingly.

---

## 4. Add, Commit & Push

```bash
# 1. Make sure you’re in the repo root
cd nodejs-welcome

# 2. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile kubernetes.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 3. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to main
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, the workflow will trigger automatically, building the Docker image and pushing it to Docker Hub (or your chosen registry).  

Happy coding! 🚀
